entities.name: philology
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Philology is the scholarly discipline concerned with the study of language through written historical and literary texts — encompassing textual criticism, literary analysis, linguistics, and historical interpretation. As one of the oldest systematic academic disciplines, philology was the primary method through which European scholars in the 18th and 19th centuries reconstructed ancient languages, identified textual corruptions, and established the comparative study of languages that became modern linguistics.

The term derives from Greek (love of language/learning). Renaissance humanist philologists — Erasmus, Lorenzo Valla, Angelo Poliziano — applied philological analysis to recover classical texts and expose forgeries (Valla proved the Donation of Constantine was a medieval forgery). 19th-century comparative philology — William Jones's identification of the Indo-European language family (1786), the Grimm Brothers' sound laws — transformed philology into a scientific discipline and gave it the methods that would become modern linguistics. Karl Lachmann's critical editing techniques established the stemmatic method of textual reconstruction still used today.

Philology's greatest achievements include the critical editions of Homer, the Bible, and the major classical and medieval corpora; the decipherment of ancient scripts (Egyptian hieroglyphics, Linear B, Cuneiform); and the reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European. The discipline's methods are essential for any rigorous engagement with texts in historical languages — it underpins biblical scholarship, classical studies, Oriental studies, medieval studies, and the emerging field of digital humanities, where computational tools are extending philological analysis to corpora of previously impossible scale.
